description: The conformance corpus for standards/025-structured-data.md. Three parts, all pure functions of their inputs so they can be written as data and run in any language. 'migrations': given a migrations directory (file names and contents) and the scripts a deploy path can reach, the findings a checker must report (SD2, SD4). 'isolation': given a product's declared isolation levels, its tables with their columns, and queries each issued in a stated context, the schema findings the checker must report (SD5) and the rows each query must and must not see (SD6). 'schema': given a declared schema - tables with typed, nullability-marked columns, indexes as ordered column lists, foreign keys, and declared types - the findings the SD10 checker must report. A finding is reported by kind and subject; an implementation reproduces every expected finding and no others, or names the case it failed.

migrations.why: SD2's shape and SD4's rule both satisfied. The Down sections contain DROP TABLE and are ignored: down migrations are for local iteration and are never trusted in production.

directory.0002_add_invoices.ts: export async function up(db) { await db.schema.createTable('invoices')... }

migrations.why: SD2. A migration is never code: an up() function puts a translation layer between the reviewer and the statement, and ties the history to a language runtime.
SD2. The name is the order. A file with no ordering prefix applies at whatever position the tool's sort puts it, which differs between tools.
SD4. The previous release may still read legacy_ref; rolling back to it against this schema is a data-loss event wearing a tag change.

directory.00007_retire_legacy_ref.sql:
-- +goose Up
-- expand-only-ok: 2.4.0 stopped reading legacy_ref
ALTER TABLE invoices DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS legacy_ref;
-- +goose Down

migrations.why: SD4. The marker names the release after which the statement became safe. That is the third release of the three the rule requires, and the reviewer can check the claim.

directory.00007_retire_legacy_ref.sql:
-- +goose Up
-- expand-only-ok:
ALTER TABLE invoices DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS legacy_ref;
-- +goose Down

migrations.why: SD4. The marker is a reason, not a permission. An empty marker is a violation with a comment on it, and a checker that accepts the token without its argument has turned the rule into a magic word.
SD4 names three statement kinds, and ALTER ... TYPE is the one people forget is destructive. The DROP TABLE in the Down section is not a finding: Down is never trusted and never gated.
SD2. Two answers to one question inside one tree, and the script named migrate is the wrong one. This is the shape found in the portfolio, not a hypothetical.

SD2's convergence rule. Re-run against a database where the table exists, this file errors instead of exiting zero - and it will be re-run, after an interrupted migrate on an engine whose DDL cannot roll back, or against a restore taken between apply and record. IF NOT EXISTS costs three words.

SD8 through SD2: a seed is a migration, so it converges. Without ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (or the engine's equivalent) the second run either duplicates the rows or fails a unique constraint, and either way the migrate step is no longer safe to repeat.

isolation.why: SD5 and SD6 in their correct shape. currencies carries no isolation column and is unscoped by declaration: reference data every tenant sees. invoices is scoped at client_org and carries tenant_id too, so its predicate needs no join.

SD5's denormalization rule, and a VERIFIED DETECTOR. deliverables is scoped at client_org and so must also carry tenant_id, because containment is declared upward and the tenant predicate must be joinless. A suite that checks only the innermost column passes this table and fails the rule; this case fails such a suite by name.

SD6. The platform host, an unauthenticated path, a job with no tenant bound: no context resolved means no scoped rows, by construction. Unscoped reference data is unaffected. An implementation that treats a null context as a wildcard fails the first query.

SD5 containment: a tenant-level context sees every row in the tenant, across its client organisations, and nothing in another tenant. Whether a particular tenant USER may see across client orgs is the authorization layer's question (RB5); the isolation layer's question is only which tenant the rows belong to.

SD5's reason for the redundant column. c1 belongs to t1; a context claiming c1 under t2 matches on the inner column and fails on the outer one. A predicate that checked only client_org_id would return the row - which is the joinless-predicate rule protecting against a forged or stale context.
SD5 fixes no depth, including zero. A single-tenant product declares no levels, nothing is scoped, and the suite has nothing to enumerate - which is a pass, not a gap.

schema.why: SD10 satisfied: every foreign key leads an index, every table carries both timestamps, no native enum, every identifier snake_case, and the scoped table's outermost isolation column leads a composite index.

SD10. tenant_id appears in an index but does not lead one, which is the case people miss: an index on (created_at, tenant_id) helps neither the foreign key nor the isolation predicate. Two findings, because the same column fails two rules.
SD10. created_at without updated_at answers one of the two questions every support call asks and not the other.
SD10. The type exists in the catalog, so the checker sees it without parsing anything. A CHECK constraint on a text column does the same job and migrates like any other constraint.

SD10. createdAt is not snake_case, and because an unquoted reference would fold it to createdat, it also fails to be the created_at the timestamp rule looks for. One mistake, two findings, which is roughly what it costs in production too.
SD5 fixes no depth, including zero, and SD10's isolation-index rule therefore has nothing to enumerate. A pass, not a gap.
